chunks: SIMO buck converter. The question: What is a single-input multiple-output (SIMO) buck converter?
SIMO usually stands for single-inductor multiple-output (the question's "single-input" wording describes the same converter from the supply side).
It makes several different output voltages from one input using just one inductor. A normal buck needs its own inductor for every output, and inductors are big and costly.
A SIMO shares the single inductor between the outputs by serving them one at a time.
Imagine one person with a watering can and three thirsty plants. They fill the can once, pour it into plant A, refill, pour it into plant B, and so on.
One can serves every plant, and the schedule decides who gets water.
The catch is that the plants share a limited supply: if one drinks a lot, the others may wait, which is called cross-regulation.
The power stage is a normal synchronous buck up to the inductor. After L , a node fans out through three output switches S 1 to S 3 , each feeding its own output capacitor.
A controller closes exactly one output switch at a time, while Q H / Q L pulse the inductor.
Output rail: one regulated voltage the converter must supply. Time-multiplexing: taking turns, one output per time slot.
Inductor: the coil that stores and moves energy in each slot ("Inductor differential equation"). Discontinuous mode: each slot ends with the inductor current back at zero.
Cross-regulation: one output's load affecting another output's voltage.
Say a device needs three rails. Three ordinary bucks need three inductors, three high-side switches and three low-side switches.
A SIMO keeps one pair of main switches and one inductor, and adds one small steering switch per output. In slot one the steering switch connects the inductor to output A.
The main switch lets the inductor current build up from the input, then lets it run down into output A until it reaches zero.
Slot two does the same for output B, and slot three for C, then it repeats. That is the whole idea.
"SIMO means single-inductor multiple-output: one input, one shared inductor, several regulated rails.
The inductor is time-multiplexed: it's charged from the input and then dumped into one output at a time, usually in discontinuous mode so each slot starts at zero current.
The win is area and cost, because one inductor replaces several.
The costs are cross-regulation between outputs, high peak inductor currents, a shared power limit, and a complex controller."
